title: Why English Examiners Struggle
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles analyses a 2018 Ofqual research report finding that English examiners achieved only 44% exact agreement on student scripts -- meaning 56% of the time, two trained examiners marking the same piece of work assigned different marks. He argues this is not a measurement problem susceptible to technical fixes but a disciplinary problem rooted in the nature of English as a subject. The Ofqual researchers identified four categories of examiner error: not applying the mark scheme consistently, not reading the whole script before marking, being influenced by performance on one question when marking another, and applying personal taste rather than published criteria. Salles treats each as a pedagogical warning: they reveal the latent criteria students should be taught to satisfy regardless of who marks their work. Salles focuses particularly on AO6 (the assessment objective for technical accuracy and writing quality in GCSE English), arguing that because examiners disagree most sharply on evaluative holistic judgments, students are best served by developing technical skills whose quality is least contestable -- vocabulary range, sentence variety, punctuation accuracy. The article's practical implication is to teach to the objective rather than to the examiner: focus on skills the mark scheme values rather than the preferences of any particular marking style. The 56% disagreement rate is an argument for teaching the objectively measurable components of writing quality with unusual rigour.
points: Ofqual's 2018 research found 56% examiner disagreement on the same student scripts -- a finding that should fundamentally reframe how English teachers think about what they are preparing students to produce and for whom.

The four examiner error categories (inconsistent mark scheme application, partial script reading, halo effects, personal-taste substitution) are also a syllabus of what to teach: skills durable enough to survive variability in the marker.

AO6 attracts the widest examiner disagreement precisely because it is evaluated holistically; teachers can reduce students' exposure to this variance by drilling sub-skills whose quality is least contestable -- sentence control, vocabulary precision, punctuation.

The examiner disagreement problem is not primarily a measurement artifact; it is evidence that English assessment contains a legitimate subjective component, and students should be taught to produce writing robust to that subjectivity.
Teaching students to write for the mark scheme is a genuine and transferable skill -- making quality legible across a diverse population of assessors -- not an act of inauthenticity.
quotes: The single most powerful finding in the Ofqual research is the 44% exact agreement rate. One in two times, two trained examiners looking at the same script disagreed on the mark. This is not a rounding error. It is the system working as designed -- and it should change how we teach.

Ofqual identified four main sources of examiner error: not applying the mark scheme consistently; not reading the whole response before beginning to mark; allowing performance on one question to influence marking of another; and substituting personal preferences for published criteria.

AO6 is where the disagreement is worst. Holistic judgments about writing quality are the hardest to standardise, because they require the examiner to weigh multiple features simultaneously against a descriptor that cannot fully specify what 'good' looks like in every possible student response.

If examiners systematically disagree about holistic writing quality, the intelligent response is to ensure your students' writing contains features about which there is relatively little disagreement: technical accuracy, vocabulary range, sentence variety.

The 56% disagreement rate does not mean English is subjective in a way that renders assessment meaningless. It means English contains a legitimate evaluative dimension that we have not yet found a way to standardise -- and that teachers who understand this can build it into their instruction.

Teaching students to write for the mark scheme is not a corruption of English education. The mark scheme is an attempt to operationalise what skilled writing looks like. Teaching students to satisfy it explicitly is teaching them what skilled writing actually requires -- made unusually legible.
